title: Software Testing · Chapter 2
description: Fundamentals of testing: what testing is, the seven principles, error vs defect vs failure, the fundamental test process, and the psychology of testing.

topics.title: What Is Testing?
topics.description: The definition of testing, testing vs debugging, and test objectives.

questions.prompt: According to the definition of testing, the lifecycle activities involved are…

options.text: Only the activities carried out after coding

questions.explanation: Testing consists of all lifecycle activities, both static (e.g. reviews) and dynamic (executing the software).

questions.prompt: According to the definition, testing evaluates a component or system and related work products in order to… (select all that apply)

options.text: Demonstrate that they are fit for purpose
Determine that they satisfy specified requirements
Prove that the software contains no defects

questions.explanation: The definition lists three aims: satisfy specified requirements, demonstrate fitness for purpose, and detect defects. Testing can never prove that defects are absent.

questions.prompt: What is the goal of debugging?

options.text: Comparing actual progress against the test plan

questions.explanation: Debugging is the task of localizing and correcting faults. Detecting failures is the goal of testing.

questions.prompt: What is the goal of testing, as opposed to debugging?

options.text: The (more or less systematic) detection of failures that indicate the presence of defects
Localizing and correcting faults in the code

questions.explanation: Testing detects failures that point to defects; debugging then localizes and corrects the faults.

questions.prompt: Testing and debugging are the same activity.
questions.explanation: They are different: testing detects failures, while debugging localizes and corrects the faults that caused them.

questions.prompt: A reason or purpose for designing and executing a test is called a test ______.
questions.explanation: A test objective is a reason or purpose for designing and executing a test.

questions.prompt: Which of these are usual test objectives? (select all that apply)

options.text: Assigning blame to the developer who wrote the code
Gaining confidence about the quality of the system and providing information

questions.explanation: The usual test objectives are finding defects, preventing defects, and gaining confidence about quality / providing information.

questions.prompt: How can testing help to PREVENT defects? (select all that apply)

options.text: Waiting until coding is finished before testing
Designing tests early in the test lifecycle
Re-running the same unchanged tests many times

questions.explanation: Designing tests early can stop defects being introduced into the code, and reviewing documents like requirements also reduces defects.

questions.prompt: Testing is concerned with the system AND its related work products, not only the program code.
questions.explanation: The definition covers a component or system and related work products, such as requirements and design documents.

topics.title: General Testing Principles
topics.description: The seven principles of testing, plus test cases.

questions.prompt: How many general testing principles are there?
questions.explanation: There are seven: presence of defects, exhaustive testing is impossible, early testing, defect clustering, pesticide paradox, context dependence, and the absence-of-errors fallacy.

questions.prompt: “Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence.” Which principle is this?
questions.explanation: Principle 1: testing shows the presence of defects. Even when no failures are found, you cannot conclude that no defects remain.

questions.prompt: Exhaustive (complete) testing is feasible for most real-world programs if enough time is available.
questions.explanation: Exhaustive testing is impossible except for trivial programs, so testing effort must be focused.

questions.prompt: Why does early testing (e.g. reviews running in parallel with development) save money?

options.text: It guarantees the software has no defects
Defects are detected earlier, and earlier defects cost less to fix
It lets you skip writing requirements
It removes the need for any later testing

questions.explanation: Testing should start as early as possible. Defects found early cost less to fix.

questions.prompt: A small number of modules contains most of the defects found during pre-release testing. Which principle describes this?
questions.explanation: Defect clustering: effort should be focused in proportion to the expected and observed defect density of modules.

questions.prompt: Running the same tests over and over eventually stops finding new defects. What is this principle also called? (two words)
questions.explanation: This is the pesticide paradox: repetitions have no effect, so tests must be reviewed and revised.

questions.prompt: What should be done to overcome the pesticide paradox?

options.text: Run the same tests more often
Stop testing once no new defects are found
Only add more testers to the team
Regularly review, revise and modify the test cases

questions.explanation: Test cases need to be regularly reviewed, revised and modified to keep finding new defects.

questions.prompt: Safety-critical software is tested more intensely, and with other techniques, than a commercial application. Which principle is this?
questions.explanation: Testing depends on context: the type of system determines how intensely and with what techniques it is tested.

questions.prompt: A system has no failures, yet users say it does not meet their expectations. Which principle explains this?
questions.explanation: Absence of errors fallacy: a system without failures does not automatically meet users' expectations.

questions.prompt: Which of the following ARE among the seven general testing principles? (select all that apply)

options.text: Testing proves that software is bug-free

questions.explanation: Early testing, defect clustering and context dependence are principles. Testing never proves software is bug-free, and exhaustive testing is impossible.

questions.prompt: What is a test case?

options.text: A set of conditions or variables under which a tester determines whether a system under test satisfies requirements or works correctly
The overall plan for the whole test project
A report describing a defect that was found
A tool used to manage tests

questions.explanation: A test case is a set of conditions or variables used to determine whether the system under test (SUT) satisfies requirements or works correctly.

questions.prompt: In the definition of a test case, what does the abbreviation SUT stand for?
questions.explanation: SUT = System Under Test.

questions.prompt: The process of developing test cases can also help find problems in the requirements or design of an application.
questions.explanation: Writing test cases forces you to read requirements and design closely, which often reveals problems in them.

questions.prompt: Companies normally use a test management tool, and the test case format is determined by that tool or the standard the company follows.
questions.explanation: There is no single universal template; the format usually comes from the test management tool or company standard.

topics.title: Why Testing Is Necessary
topics.description: Error, defect and failure; causes and costs of defects; testing and quality.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows how a problem moves from a person, into the software, and then into operation. Which sequence of terms matches Steps 1 → 2 → 3?

image.alt: Three boxes joined by arrows: Step 1 shows a person, Step 2 shows the software (code symbol), Step 3 shows a broken screen labelled 'In operation'.
image.caption: Step 1 → Step 2 → Step 3

questions.explanation: A person makes an ERROR, which creates a FAULT (defect) in the software, which can cause a FAILURE in operation.

questions.prompt: “A human action that produces an incorrect result.” This is the definition of…
questions.explanation: An error, or mistake, is a human action that produces an incorrect result.

questions.prompt: “A flaw in a component or system that can cause it to fail to perform its required function, e.g. an incorrect statement or data definition.” This is…
questions.explanation: A defect (fault or bug) is a flaw in a component or system, such as an incorrect statement or data definition.

questions.prompt: A discrepancy between the actual result (seen while executing a test) and the expected result (from the specification) is called…
questions.explanation: A failure is a non-fulfilment of a requirement: the actual result or behaviour differs from what was expected.

questions.prompt: A defect always causes a failure.
questions.explanation: A defect MAY cause a failure, but only if it is encountered during execution.

questions.prompt: A product that is too slow or too hard to use can count as a failure even if it fulfils all its functional requirements.
questions.explanation: A failure is present when a warrantable user expectation is not fulfilled adequately, e.g. a system that is too slow or too hard to use.

questions.prompt: Which of these are causes of the human errors that lead to defects? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The notes list time pressure, complex code, complex infrastructure, changed technology and too many system interactions.

questions.prompt: Ariane 5 self-destructed 39 seconds after take-off on its maiden flight (4 June 1996). What was the cause?

options.text: The rotation of the earth around the sun was not taken into consideration
Ozone measurements were averaged out by the software
Ariane 4 position control software was reused without testing against Ariane 5's take-off trajectory, causing a conversion error

questions.explanation: The Ariane 4 position control software was reused for Ariane 5 without being tested against the new trajectory, leading to a conversion error.

questions.prompt: The manned NASA capsule Gemini V missed its airfield by about 160 km. What was the software defect?

options.text: The rotation of the earth around the sun was not taken into consideration
Software from an earlier rocket was reused without testing
A unit conversion between metres and feet

questions.explanation: Gemini V's software did not account for the earth's rotation around the sun.

questions.prompt: Because of a software defect in NASA's Earth observation satellites (1979–1985), for how many years was the hole in the ozone layer not detected?
questions.explanation: The hole in the ozone layer went undetected for 7 years.

questions.prompt: What are implications of defects in software? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Defects can cause loss of money, waste of time, damage to reputation, and even injury or death.

questions.prompt: What is the role of software testing in development, maintenance and operation? (select all that apply)

options.text: It guarantees that no defects will ever occur in operation
It may be required to meet contractual, legal or industry-specific standards
Rigorous testing helps reduce risks during operation of the system
It contributes to quality if defects are found and corrected before release

questions.explanation: Testing reduces risk, contributes to quality when defects are fixed before release, and may be required by contracts, law or standards. It cannot guarantee zero defects.

questions.prompt: Testing can give confidence in the quality of a system if few or no defects are found.
questions.explanation: When few or no defects are found, testing gives confidence in the system's quality.

questions.prompt: According to the notes, when does the quality of the system actually increase?

options.text: When the test plan is approved
When the defects that were found are fixed
As soon as defects are found
When more test cases are written

questions.explanation: Finding defects only measures quality. Quality increases when those defects are fixed.

questions.prompt: Complete the flow: Root cause analysis of previous defects → ______ → Prevents defects in future → Improves quality of the system.
questions.explanation: Root cause analysis leads to process improvement, which prevents future defects and improves quality.

questions.prompt: Testing is a part of Quality Assurance (QA).
questions.explanation: Testing is one aspect of QA.

topics.title: Fundamental Test Process
topics.description: Planning & control, analysis & design, implementation & execution, exit criteria, closure.

questions.prompt: Which activity of the fundamental test process belongs in the box marked “?”

image.alt: Flow of five numbered boxes: 1 Planning and control, 2 Analysis and design, 3 is a dashed box with a question mark, 4 Evaluating exit criteria and reporting, 5 Test closure activities.
image.caption: Fundamental test process

questions.explanation: The five activities are: 1 Planning and control, 2 Analysis and design, 3 Implementation and execution, 4 Evaluating exit criteria and reporting, 5 Test closure activities (PAIET).

questions.prompt: What 5-letter acronym from the notes helps you remember the fundamental test process activities?
questions.explanation: PAIET = Planning & control, Analysis & design, Implementation & execution, Evaluating exit criteria & reporting, Test closure.

questions.prompt: Which of these are activities of the fundamental test process? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Debugging and deployment are not part of the fundamental test process.

questions.prompt: Verifying the mission of testing, defining the objectives of testing and specifying test activities to meet them is called…
questions.explanation: Test planning verifies the mission, defines the objectives and specifies the test activities.

questions.prompt: The ongoing activity of comparing actual progress against the plan, reporting status (including deviations) and taking necessary actions is called…
questions.explanation: Test control continuously compares actual progress against the plan and takes action when needed.

questions.prompt: In which activity are general testing objectives transformed into tangible test conditions and test cases?
questions.explanation: Test analysis and design turns general objectives into concrete test conditions and test cases.

questions.prompt: Which are major tasks of test ANALYSIS and DESIGN? (select all that apply)

options.text: Handing testware over to the maintenance organisation
Writing a test summary report for stakeholders
Evaluating testability of the test basis and test objects

questions.explanation: REIDID: Review test basis, Evaluate testability, Identify & prioritise test conditions, Design & prioritise test cases, Identify test data, Design test environment. The summary report and handover belong to later activities.

questions.prompt: Requirements, architecture, design and interfaces that are reviewed during test analysis are together known as the test ______.
questions.explanation: The test basis is the documentation that tests are derived from.

questions.prompt: Which activity combines test cases into test procedures/scripts in a particular order, sets up the environment and runs the tests?
questions.explanation: Implementation and execution: procedures are specified, the environment is set up and the tests are run.

questions.prompt: Which are major tasks of test IMPLEMENTATION and EXECUTION? (select all that apply)

options.text: Verifying that the test environment is set up correctly
Comparing actual results with expected results
Creating test suites from the test procedures
Checking test logs against the exit criteria

questions.explanation: Checking logs against exit criteria belongs to evaluating exit criteria; archiving testware belongs to test closure.

questions.prompt: During execution, discrepancies between actual and expected results are reported as ______.
questions.explanation: Discrepancies are reported as incidents and analysed to find their cause.

questions.prompt: Re-executing a test that previously failed, in order to confirm that a fix works, is called…
questions.explanation: Confirmation testing re-runs a previously failed test to confirm the fix.

questions.prompt: Running tests to make sure that defects have not been introduced into UNCHANGED areas of the software (or that a fix did not uncover other defects) is called…
questions.explanation: Regression testing checks that changes have not broken areas that were not changed.

questions.prompt: Which are major tasks of EVALUATING EXIT CRITERIA and REPORTING? (select all that apply)

options.text: Checking test logs against the exit criteria specified in test planning
Assessing if more tests are needed or if the exit criteria should be changed
Writing a test summary report for stakeholders

questions.explanation: Exit-criteria evaluation checks logs, decides if more tests or changed criteria are needed, and produces the summary report.

questions.prompt: Evaluating exit criteria should be done for each test level.
questions.explanation: Exit criteria are evaluated at every test level, not just once at the end.

questions.prompt: Which are major tasks of TEST CLOSURE activities? (select all that apply)

options.text: Analysing lessons learned for future projects
Handing over testware to the maintenance organisation
Executing test procedures in the planned sequence
Finalising and archiving testware, the test environment and infrastructure for reuse
Checking which planned deliverables have been delivered

questions.explanation: Executing test procedures is part of implementation and execution, not closure.

questions.prompt: Which events can trigger test closure activities? (select all that apply)

options.text: A new tester joins the team
A maintenance release has been completed
A test project is completed or cancelled

questions.explanation: Closure collects data when a system is released, a project ends or is cancelled, a milestone is reached, or a maintenance release is completed.

topics.title: The Psychology of Testing
topics.description: Tester and developer mindsets, and how to communicate well.

questions.prompt: Why are the mindsets of testers and developers different? (select all that apply)

options.text: Testers should criticise developers personally to improve quality
Testers can provide an independent view
Errors/defects should be communicated in a constructive way

questions.explanation: Testers bring independence and avoid author bias, but must communicate constructively with good interpersonal skills.

questions.prompt: Independent testing helps to avoid ______ bias.
questions.explanation: Independent testing avoids author bias: authors tend to overlook their own mistakes.

questions.prompt: What is the best way for a tester to report a defect to a developer?

options.text: Communicate the finding in a neutral, fact-focused way without criticising the person who created it
Point out who made the mistake so it doesn't happen again
Escalate it to management before talking to the developer
Only mention it informally so nobody is upset

questions.explanation: Findings should be neutral and fact-focused, about the product, not the person.

questions.prompt: Which are tips for improving communication between testers and developers? (select all that apply)

options.text: Win every argument about whether something is a defect
Confirm the other person has understood what you said, and vice versa
Try to understand how the other person feels and why they react as they do
Start with collaboration rather than battles

questions.explanation: Collaborate, empathise, and confirm mutual understanding — remembering the shared goal of better quality.

questions.prompt: Testers and developers share a common goal: better quality systems.
questions.explanation: Reminding everyone of this common goal is the first tip for good collaboration.
